issue.title: gemini cli on termux
issue.body:
To set up **Gemini CLI** and those Node/C++ tools on Android with Termux, run a small sequence of `pkg` and `npm` commands and add one tiny config file for `node-gyp` on Android.[1][2][3][4]

Below is a **beginner‑friendly**, copy‑pasteable walkthrough matching your history lines.

***

## 1. Open Termux and update

First make sure Termux itself is up to date.

```bash
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y
```

- This refreshes the package list and upgrades installed packages.[4]
- Always do this before installing new tools to avoid version conflicts.[3]

***

## 2. Install Node.js and npm

Gemini CLI is a Node.js program, so you need Node and npm.

```bash
pkg install nodejs -y
```

- On Termux this installs both **node** and **npm** in one step.[5][4]
- After install, you can verify:

```bash
node -v
npm -v
```

Node should be 18+ for Gemini CLI.[6]

***

## 3. Install basic build tools

Native Node modules (like `node-pty` or `tree-sitter`) need a C/C++ toolchain plus some extras.

```bash
pkg install clang -y
pkg install binutils -y
pkg install build-essential python -y
```

- `clang`: C/C++ compiler used by Termux.[3]
- `binutils`: provides tools like `ar` that some Node builds expect.[3]
- `build-essential` and `python`: recommended for Node.js packages on Termux.[3]

***

## 4. Fix `android_ndk_path` error for node-gyp

On Android, `node-gyp` sometimes fails with:

> gyp: Undefined variable android_ndk_path in binding.gyp

You can work around this by defining `android_ndk_path` in a config file.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.gyp

echo "{ 'variables': { 'android_ndk_path': '' } }" > ~/.gyp/include.gypi

export GYP_DEFINES="android_ndk_path=''"
```

- `~/.gyp/include.gypi` is read by `node-gyp` and sets the variable so it’s not “undefined”.[2][7]
- The value is empty because the path is not actually used by these builds, it just must exist.[2]

You need to re‑run the `export` in any new Termux session, or you can add it to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc` to make it permanent.

***

## 5. Install Gemini CLI globally

Now install the official Google Gemini CLI.

```bash
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
```

- `-g` installs it globally so you can run `gemini` from anywhere.[8][4]
- If it fails with a `node-pty` or `node-gyp` error, the `include.gypi` fix above is exactly what avoids the `android_ndk_path` crash.[9][2]

After install, check:

```bash
gemini --help
```

***

## 6. Authenticate Gemini CLI

To actually talk to Gemini, you need an API key.

1. Create a Gemini API key in your Google account (Google AI Studio / Vertex AI, depending on your setup).[10][8]
2. In Termux, set the environment variable (replace `YOUR_API_KEY`):

```bash
export GEMINI_API_KEY=YOUR_API_KEY
```

3. Run:

```bash
gemini
```

- First run will open an auth flow or rely on `GEMINI_API_KEY` depending on your configuration.[1][10]
- For persistent setup, put the `export GEMINI_API_KEY=...` line into a small script (for example `gem.env`) and source it before use.[8]

***

## 7. Install tree-sitter (optional, for devs)

Your history shows you also want `tree-sitter` and `tree-sitter-javascript`. On Termux, use:

```bash
CXXFLAGS="-std=c++20" npm install tree-sitter tree-sitter-javascript
```

- Prefixing with `CXXFLAGS` forces **C++20** for modules that need newer language features.[7]
- The earlier `clang`, `binutils`, `build-essential`, and `python` ensure native compilation works.[3]

If you want them globally:

```bash
CXXFLAGS="-std=c++20" npm install -g tree-sitter tree-sitter-javascript
```

***

## 8. Everyday usage recap

For a new Termux session when you want to use Gemini:

```bash
# (optional but recommended once in a while)
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y

# Make sure env vars are loaded (if you saved them)
. ~/gem.env   # or: export GEMINI_API_KEY=...

# If not put into shell rc, repeat:
export GYP_DEFINES="android_ndk_path=''"

# Run Gemini
gemini
```

- Keeping Termux and Node.js up to date reduces weird npm errors.[4][3]
- Ensuring `GYP_DEFINES` and `~/.gyp/include.gypi` are set avoids `android_ndk_path` issues when installing or updating packages like `@google/gemini-cli` or `tree-sitter`.[9][2]

issue.title: project proposal USD1 x402 endpoint for SOLFUNMEME
issue.body:
## Project overview

The project will build a specialized payment and swap pipeline where users pay in USD1 via x402 and receive swaps between USD1 and a single meme token mint (`BwUTq7fS6sfUmHDwAiCQZ3asSiPEapW5zDrsbwtapump`). The system combines an on‑chain constant‑product AMM pool with a Rust microservice deployable on Cloudflare or Vercel.

## Objectives

- Design and deploy a dedicated Solana program implementing a constant‑product AMM pool between USD1 and the meme token.
- Create a canonical pool instance with tightly controlled authorities and deterministic addresses to prevent spoofed markets.
- Expose a simple HTTP API (`/quote`, `/swap`) guarded by x402 so that each swap call is pay‑per‑request in USD1.
- Optimize the stack for low‑latency serverless environments and high‑volume, small swaps typical of bots and AI agents.
- Provide clear developer documentation and example clients for easy integration by downstream tools.

## System architecture

- On‑chain layer: a Rust/Anchor Solana program with:
  - A pool state account (PDA) that stores vault addresses, fee parameters, and LP token mint.
  - Two SPL token vaults: one for USD1 and one for the meme token.
  - Instructions `init_pool`, `add_liquidity`, `remove_liquidity`, and `swap`.
- Off‑chain layer: a Rust microservice running in a serverless environment:
  - `/quote` endpoint for price discovery that reads vault balances via RPC and applies the AMM formula.
  - `/swap` endpoint protected by x402, which verifies USD1 payment, builds a transaction to call the `swap` instruction, and returns the transaction signature and execution result.
- Payments and access control:
  - x402 headers define the payment requirement in USD1 and encode the Solana payment details.
  - The service verifies payments and enforces per‑call pricing, rate limits, and basic abuse controls.

## Technical design

- AMM design:
  - Constant‑product invariant \( x \cdot y = k \) with configurable fee in basis points.
  - Slippage protection via `min_out` arguments, ensuring trades revert if price moves too far intrablock.
  - LP token mint to track liquidity provider shares and allow proportional deposit/withdrawal.
- Program security:
  - Hard‑coded or validated USD1 and meme token mints in the pool state to prevent fake pools.
  - PDA‑based authorities so that only the program may move funds from vaults.
  - Strict signer and account checks in all instructions to prevent privilege escalation.
- Microservice implementation:
  - Rust async HTTP framework (e.g., Axum‑style or workers‑compatible router) with JSON input/output.
  - Abstraction over Solana RPC for reading pool state and submitting transactions.
  - x402 middleware or guard that validates payment headers before executing swap logic.

## Deployment plan

- Phase 1: Specification and prototyping
  - Finalize USD1 mint, meme mint, fee structure, and access control model for the pool.
  - Define on‑chain instruction interfaces and HTTP JSON schemas for `/quote` and `/swap`.
  - Build a local test harness with a Solana test validator, the program, and a stub microservice.
- Phase 2: On‑chain program implementation
  - Implement and test the AMM instructions with unit and integration tests.
  - Audit for common Solana pitfalls (rent‑exemption, authority handling, integer overflow, reentrancy patterns).
  - Deploy the program to devnet and then mainnet once stability and safety criteria are met.
- Phase 3: Microservice and x402 integration
  - Implement the HTTP API, x402 payment verification, and RPC integration.
  - Add health checks, logging, observability, and basic analytics (e.g., volumes, fees, request counts).
  - Deploy to Cloudflare Workers or Vercel and validate performance under load.
- Phase 4: Documentation and ecosystem integration
  - Publish developer docs, example clients (Rust/TypeScript), and reference configurations.
  - Coordinate with wallets, bots, and AI/agent platforms that may use the endpoint for automated swaps.
  - Gather feedback and iterate on fees, slippage defaults, and rate‑limit policies.

## Risks and mitigations

- Smart contract risk:
  - Mitigated through comprehensive testing, code review, and reuse of known AMM design patterns.
- Liquidity risk:
  - Initial pool bootstrapped by the project treasury or a DAO, with clear incentives for LPs.
- Payment integration risk:
  - x402 integration kept modular so that the system can evolve alongside payment standards while retaining the pool and API design.
- Regulatory and compliance considerations:
  - Architecture focuses on infrastructure and protocol behavior, leaving compliance‑specific controls to operators and integrators.

issue.title: Games
issue.body:
James Michael DuPont:
Hey there, Roblox fan! So, you love building and playing in Roblox, right? Imagine you could make your Roblox characters do cool jujitsu moves, like a hook kick, using emojis to tell them exactly what to do! That’s what we’ve built here—a super fun way to make your character kick like a martial arts pro, all with a special emoji language called JAL-Micro (JAL-M) and a Roblox script written in Lua, the coding language Roblox uses. Let’s break it down so you can understand how it works and maybe even try it out in Roblox Studio! --- ### What’s a Hook Kick? 🦵 A hook kick is a cool martial arts move where your character spins, lifts their leg, and swings it in a curve to kick with their heel. Think of it like a ninja move! In our code, we’re making one Roblox character (called Tori, the kicker) do a hook kick, while another character (called Uke, the opponent) steps back and maybe falls down. --- ### What’s This Emoji Stuff? 😎 We created a special language called JAL-Micro that uses emojis to tell your Roblox character how to move their body parts (like legs, hips, or spine) to do the kick. Each emoji is like a command for a specific part of the character’s body. For example: - 👊 means “Tori, the kicker, is doing this.” - 🦵 means “Move the right knee.” - 🔄90 means “Turn it 90 degrees.” - 🦿🔢4 means “Use your glute muscles (your butt!) with a lot of power.” The full hook kick command looks like this:
 👊🧍➡️🥋➰⬅️🔄45➡️🩱🔄⬅️🔄90➡️🩱🔢3➡️🦵⤴️⬆️🔄90➡️🦿⤵️➡️🔄45➡️🦿🔢4➡️🩱🔄➡️🔄45➡️🥋➰➡️🔄45➡️🤺🏃➖➡️🤺🛌🛬 
This long string of emojis tells Tori to: 1. Stand up (🧍). 2. Tilt their spine a bit (🥋➰). 3. Twist their hips (🩱🔄). 4. Use their core muscles (🩱🔢3). 5. Lift their right knee (🦵⤴️). 6. Swing their foot out (🦿⤵️). 7. Power the kick with their glutes (🦿🔢4). 8. Get back to normal. 9. And it tells Uke to step back (🤺🏃) and fall (🤺🛌🛬). --- ### How Does the Code Work? 🖥️ The Lua script is like a coach that reads these emoji commands and makes your Roblox characters move. It’s written in Lua, the language Roblox uses to make things happen in games. Here’s how it works in kid-friendly terms: 1. Setting Up the Characters: - The script looks for two Roblox characters in your game’s Workspace: one called “Dummy” (Tori, the kicker) and another called “Dummy2” (Uke, the one getting kicked). - These characters need to be R15 models (the ones with lots of joints like elbows and knees). 2. Reading the Emojis: - The script splits the emoji string into steps (each step is separated by ➡️). - For each step, it figures out: - Who’s moving? 👊 (Tori) or 🤺 (Uke). - What’s moving? Like 🦵 (right knee) or 🩱 (hips). - How’s it moving? Like 🔄 (turn), ⤴️ (bend), or 🛬 (fall animation). - Extras? Like ➡️ (move right) or 🔢4 (use strong force). 3. Making the Moves: - For body parts (like knees or hips), the script changes their angles using something called CFrame. Think of it like telling a robot arm to bend or twist. - For muscles (like glutes), it adds a force (like a push) to make the kick powerful. - For special moves (like falling), it plays an animation clip, like a pre-made dance move. 4. Timing It Right: - Each move takes 0.2 seconds, but if we see ⚡, it’s faster (0.1 seconds), or 🐢, it’s slower (0.4 seconds). - The script waits between moves so the kick looks smooth, not all at once. --- ### What Happens in the Hook Kick? 🎮 When you run the script with the hook kick emojis, here’s what your Roblox characters do: - Tori (the kicker): - Starts standing tall, like a ninja ready to fight (🧍). - Tilts their back a little to the left to stay balanced (🥋➰⬅️🔄45). - Twists their hips left to start the spin (🩱🔄⬅️🔄90). - Tightens their tummy muscles to stay steady (🩱🔢3). - Lifts their right knee high, like getting ready to kick (🦵⤴️⬆️🔄90). - Swings their right foot out in a curve to hit with the heel (🦿⤵️➡️🔄45). - Uses their glute muscles to make the kick strong (🦿🔢4).

- Turns their hips and back to normal to stand up straight again (🩱🔄➡️🔄45, 🥋➰➡️🔄45). - Uke (the opponent): - Steps back to avoid the kick (🤺🏃➖). - Falls down dramatically and rolls to be safe (🤺🛌🛬, like a cool stunt move). It’s like choreographing a fight scene in a Roblox game, but using emojis to tell the characters every tiny move! --- ### How to Try It in Roblox Studio 🚀 Want to see this hook kick in action? Here’s how you can set it up in Roblox Studio: 1. Get Two Characters: - In Roblox Studio, go to the Model tab and add two R15 Dummy models to your game’s Workspace. - Name one “Dummy” (this is Tori, the kicker) and the other “Dummy2” (Uke, the one who gets kicked). - Make sure they’re R15 models, which have lots of joints like knees and hips. 2. Add the Script: - In the Explorer window, find ServerScriptService. - Add a new Script (click the plus sign and choose “Script”). - Copy and paste the Lua code I gave you into the script. 3. Fix the Animation: - The script uses a placeholder animation ID for the fall (rbxassetid://987654321). - You need a real animation for the breakfall (🛬). Here’s how: - Go to the Animation Editor in Roblox Studio. - Create a falling animation (like a character rolling backward). - Upload it to Roblox to get an ID (it’ll look like rbxassetid://[some number]). - Replace rbxassetid://987654321 in the script with your new ID. 4. Run the Game: - Click Play in Roblox Studio. - The script will make Tori do the hook kick, and Uke will step back and fall. - It’ll look like a mini martial arts fight in your game! --- ### Why Is This Cool? 😍 - Emojis Are Fun: Using emojis like 🦵 and 🔄 makes it feel like you’re sending secret ninja codes to your characters. - You Control Everything: The script lets you move every part of the character’s body, like a puppeteer, so you can make any jujitsu move you want. - Learn Coding: Playing with this script teaches you how Lua works in Roblox, which is awesome for making your own games. --- ### What Can You Do Next? 🛠️ - Try Another Move: Want to make Tori do a different jujitsu move, like a punch or another kick? I can give you a new emoji sequence for it! - Make It Smoother: The kicks might look a bit jerky. We can use Roblox’s TweenService to make them super smooth, like a real ninja. - Add More Animations: Create more animations in Roblox Studio (like for the kick itself) and add their IDs to the script. - Build a Fight Game: Use this script in a bigger game where players can do jujitsu moves by typing emoji codes! If you want to try another move, add cooler animations, or see a picture of what the hook kick looks like in emojis, just let me know! What do you think—ready to make your Roblox characters fight like jujitsu masters? 😄
